title: Madhava Ghosha
html:
"The Singer of Vrindavana"

Madhava Ghosha is one of the three Ghosha brothers, an eternal companion of Sri Chaitanya and Nityananda, a kirtaniya to whose singing They danced. He is most often called Madhava Ghosha or, with reverence, Sri Madhava Ghosha Thakura; but Kavi Karnapura in the “Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika” and Vrindavana Dasa Thakura in the “Chaitanya-bhagavata” also call him Madhavananda, and under this name too — Madhavananda Ghosha Thakura — he is known in the biographies.

The finest praise of him comes from Vrindavana Dasa. Telling how Nityananda wished to dance in Panihati and the best singers gathered around Him, he names Madhava before all the rest:

“The pious Madhava Ghosha was the most skilled in singing kirtana. In this he had no equal in all the world. People call him the singer of the Lord's pastimes in Vrindavana, and he was very dear to Lord Nityananda.” (CB, Antya 5.257–258)

"The singer of Vrindavana" is not praise of a performer's craft. Madhava sang of the eternal pastimes of Vrindavana, and there was nothing worldly in his singing; that is why the Vaishnavas called him so. One biography stresses that these words come from Vrindavana Dasa himself, the servant of Nityananda.

Rasollasa

Who the three brothers are in Krishna's eternal pastimes is revealed by Kavi Karnapura:

“Kalavati, Rasollasa and Gunatunga, who were in Vraja and sang the songs composed by Sri Vishakha, are now considered to be Govinda, Madhavananda and Vasudeva respectively.” (GGD 188)1

In Vraja, then, Madhava is the sakhi Rasollasa, one of those who sang the songs composed by Sri Vishakha. Song is his eternal service; in Gaura's pastimes he continues it, glorifying the Lord in kirtana.

Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura, in the “Gaudiya-bhashya” on the “Chaitanya-bhagavata,” speaks of the brothers more deeply still: Madhava, Vasudeva and Govinda are kaya-vyuha, personal expansions of the ashraya-vigraha of the sweet madhura-rasa of Vraja, that is, of Sri Radha. Ashraya is the "abode" of love, she in whose heart love for Krishna reaches its summit. Therefore, as one biography relates, all three brothers abide in madhurya-rasa, among those who have accepted Srimati Radhika as the highest shelter of that love. This is not reincarnation in the worldly sense, nor worldly femininity, but the eternal spiritual nature of a companion who descended together with the Lord.

The Three Brothers

Madhava is the brother of Govinda Ghosha and of Vasudeva (Vasu) Ghosha. Which of the three was the eldest the sources do not say. Kavi Karnapura and Krishnadasa Kaviraja name them in the order "Govinda, Madhava, Vasudeva," and Vrindavana Dasa in the order "Madhava, Govinda, Vasudeva."

The brothers came from the kayasthas of Uttara-Rarhi — northern Rarh; according to one biography, from the part of Rarh through which the Ganga does not flow. Srila Bhaktisiddhanta too, in the “Anubhashya,” calls them kayasthas of Uttara-Rarhi2. The family was prominent and respected and belonged to the "shaukra," kayasthas by birth. The family is linked with Shrihatta (Sylhet) through the village of Buran, or Burangi; the brothers' father settled in Kumarahatta, and later the brothers moved to Navadvipa. More on this is told in the article on Vasu Ghosha3.

Krishnadasa Kaviraja in the “Chaitanya-charitamrita” calls the three brothers branches of Sri Chaitanya's tree, and at once he recalls their kirtana:

“Govinda, Madhava and Vasudeva were three brothers, and when they sang kirtana, Chaitanya and Nitai danced.” (CC, Adi 10.115)4

But Madhava is a branch of Nityananda's tree as well. Listing Nityananda's companions, Kaviraja Gosvami says that Abhirama and Gadadhara Dasa are counted in two communities at once — among the devotees of Sri Chaitanya and among the devotees of Nityananda — and adds:

“Therefore they are counted in both groups, and so it is with Madhava and Vasudeva Ghosha.” (CC, Adi 11.15)

One biography explains: in serving Nityananda in Gauda, Madhava served Gaura as well, for he went to Gauda at the command of the Lord Himself.

In Nilachala

When the devotees of Gauda first came to the Lord in Puri, King Prataparudra watched them from the palace roof, and Gopinatha Acharya named each of them for him. He pointed out the brothers too:

“Here are Govinda, Madhava Ghosha and Vasu Ghosha — three brothers whose kirtana delights the Lord.” (CC, Madhya 11.88)

At the Ratha-yatra Mahaprabhu divided the singers into seven groups, and the brothers sang in the fourth:

“He formed another group with Govinda Ghosha as the leader, in which Haridasa, Vishnudasa and Raghava sang, with the two brothers Madhava and Vasudeva Ghosha; and Vakreshvara Pandita danced there.” (CC, Madhya 13.42–43)

Srila Bhaktisiddhanta in the “Anubhashya” on Adi 10.115 says the same: in one of the seven groups these three brothers were the chief singers5.

When the Lord wished to dance Himself, He brought all seven groups together, and for His wild, leaping dance He put nine devotees with Svarupa Damodara: Srivasa, Ramai, Raghu, Govinda, Mukunda, Haridasa, Govindananda, Madhava and Govinda (CC, Madhya 13.72–74). One biography takes one of the Govindas in this list to be Govinda Ghosha; whether this Madhava is Madhava Ghosha neither that biography nor the “Charitamrita” itself specifies6.

From then on, every year the three brothers went from Gauda to Nilachala — together with Shivananda Sena and the other devotees of Bengal — and came for the Ratha-yatra; with their kirtana they increased the Lord's joy. Of the third year of these journeys the “Chaitanya-charitamrita” says:

“Acharyaratna, Vidyanidhi, Srivasa, Ramai, Vasudeva, Murari, and Govinda with his two brothers set out. Raghava Pandita packed his bags (jhali) for the journey, and the residents of Kulina-grama came bringing silk ropes.” (CC, Madhya 16.16–17)

With Nityananda in Bengal

Later Mahaprabhu sent Nityananda to preach in Gauda, Bengal. Madhava and Vasudeva went with Him, and Govinda stayed with the Lord:

“At the Lord’s command Nityananda went to Gauda, and by the Lord’s command three devotees went with Him: Sri Ramadasa, Madhava and Vasudeva Ghosha. Govinda stayed with the Lord, and was overjoyed to do so.” (CC, Adi 10.117–118)

One biography, speaking of Nityananda's coming from Nilachala to Gauda, likewise reminds us that He went at Gaura's command.

On this journey Nityananda came to Panihati, a village on the bank of the Ganga, and stayed in the house of Raghava Pandita, to the joy of Raghava, Makaradhvaja Kara and their families. Absorbed within Himself, He roared again and again, and when the desire to dance arose in His heart, the best singers gathered around, and first among them was Madhava. Vrindavana Dasa goes on:

“The three brothers — Madhava, Govinda and Vasudeva — began to sing, and Lord Nitai danced.” (CB, Antya 5.259)

Nityananda danced so that the earth trembled under the weight of His body; He loudly sang the holy name, and whoever His glance fell upon fell to the ground, overwhelmed with divine love (CB, Antya 5.260–262). To the singing of Madhava Ghosha, the best kirtaniya on earth, Nityananda danced with a thunderous roar, and then He sat on the throne of Vishnu and ordered Raghava to perform His abhisheka7. Thus Madhava, together with his brothers, took part in one of Nityananda's great festivals.

Srila Bhaktisiddhanta, in the “Gaudiya-bhashya” on the verses about Madhava, explains why the brothers were called "singers of Vrindavana": they were wholly given to kirtana and did not look on it with worldly eyes, as worldly kirtaniyas do. The inclination to serve Hari grows in the heart only when worldly conceptions have been destroyed completely; such was the kirtana of the three brothers8.

All the while Nityananda preached in Gauda, Madhava and Vasu Ghosha served Him with their singing: He danced, they led the kirtana. Krishnadasa Kaviraja speaks of Madhava in particular:

“Sri Madhava Ghosha was foremost among the kirtana singers, and Nityananda Prabhu would dance to his singing.” (CC, Adi 11.18)

The Dana-khanda in the House of Gadadhara Dasa

Especially memorable is Madhava's kirtana in Ariadaha, in the house of Gadadhara Dasa. Nityananda came there with His companions and, seeing the Deity of Bala-Gopala whom Gadadhara served, pressed Him to His chest and with a roar broke into dance in the mood of a cowherd boy (CB, Antya 5.375–377). Then Madhava began to sing:

“Then Madhavananda Ghosha sang of the dana-lila, and the lion-like avadhuta Nityananda was deeply pleased. So sweet was the voice of the fortunate Madhava that the jewel of avadhutas was filled with bliss.” (CB, Antya 5.378–379)

Dana-keli is Krishna's eternal pastime with the gopis: Krishna and His friends block the path of the girls carrying milk products to market and demand a "toll" from them; Srila Rupa Gosvami described it in the “Dana-keli-kaumudi.” This song, the dana-khanda, is what Madhava sang, and Nityananda, hearing of the dana-lila, danced so that it cannot be described; His dance was adorned with every sign of divine love (CB, Antya 5.382–383). Thus Nityananda revealed this lila through Madhava's kirtana and His own dance, and the “Charitamrita” says:

“Gadadhara Dasa was full of bliss in the mood of a gopi, and in his house Nityananda revealed the dana-keli pastime.” (CC, Adi 11.17)

From that time the temple of Gadadhara Dasa has been renowned as the site of the dana-lila, for there, when Madhavananda Ghosha sang of it, an extraordinary bhava appeared in Nityananda. Nityananda stayed with Gadadhara for several days (CB, Antya 5.393), heard the dana-khanda from Madhavananda's lips and bestowed His mercy on many. This lila is no worldly spectacle and no theatre: Madhava sang and enacted Krishna's pastime in kirtana, and Nityananda, listening, revealed it in His dance9.

Jayananda too remembers it in his “Chaitanya-mangala”: listing the wonders of Nityananda's companions in Gauda, he says: "Gadadhara Dasa makes everyone dance in his house; the singer Madhava Ghosha sings the Dana-khanda."

Songs and the Memory of the Vaishnavas

All three brothers sang with sweet voices and composed padas. As a poet Vasudeva is the best known of them; of Govinda's and Madhava's songs only a few have survived.

Yet Madhava's name lives on in the obeisances of the Vaishnavas. Lochana Dasa at the beginning of the “Chaitanya-mangala” writes: "To Govinda and Madhava Ghosha and to Vasu Ghosha, falling to the ground, with joined palms, I bow" (Sutra-khanda 34), and listing the companions who descended with the Lord, he names them as well: "Govinda, Madhava Ghosha and Vasu Ghosha — all came together and spread [bhakti] over the earth" (Sutra-khanda 629). Devakinandana in the “Vaishnava-vandana” glorifies him thus: "I shall praise Madhava Ghosha — the object of the Lord's love, to whom the Lord granted a voice that never breaks" (part 2, 81); the sweetness of his singing is the Lord's gift. In the "First Vandana," ascribed to Vrindavana Dasa, he is called "the singer Madhavananda Ghosha Mahashaya" (part 4, 65), just as Vrindavana Dasa himself, in his list of Nityananda's companions, says: "Madhavananda Ghosha Mahashaya was a singer" (CB, Antya 5.750). And Narahari Chakravarti opens the “Bhakti-ratnakara” with "Glory to Sri Mukunda, Vasu, Madhava and Shankara!" — this Madhava, too, is Madhava Ghosha.

Other vandanas glorify the three brothers as well. The Sanskrit vandana ascribed to Jiva Gosvami praises "Govinda, Madhavananda and Vasu Ghosha — treasuries of virtue" (part 1, 93); Devakinandana in the “Sri Vaishnavabhidhana” remembers "Govinda, Madhava and Vasudeva, bearing the name Ghosha" (part 3, 30); and the vandana in tripadi of the "second" Vrindavana Dasa adds: "Govinda, Madhavananda, Vasudeva Ghosha — I praise [them], three brothers, an ocean of virtues: hearing their song, Lord Vishvambhara, [surrounded by] all His associates, could not contain Himself" (part 5, 67). In the “Narottama-vilasa” of Narahari Chakravarti, Navadvipa appears to Narottama in a dream: on the bank of the Ganga Gaura, Nityananda and Advaita perform sankirtana with the devotees, and among them are "Govinda, Madhava, Vasu Ghosha" (2.122).

One biography also tells of the Navadvipa days: when Advaita performed arati to Gauranga and Gadadhara beneath a tree, "Madhava, Vasudeva, Purushottama, Vijaya, Mukunda and others" sang in various ragas. Whether this is the same Madhava the book does not say. The scene comes from a pada signed "Narahari" that the “Bhakti-ratnakara” cites, and there it reads: "Madhava, Vasu Ghosha, Purushottama, Vijaya, Mukunda…" — Vasu Ghosha is named beside Madhava, and the Ghosha brothers are apparently meant.

The Last Years

Little is known of Madhava's later years, and the accounts differ. His shripata is in Daihat, between Navadvipa and Katwa; Vasudeva settled in Tamoluk, Govinda in Agradvipa. According to one biography, "some say" that after the Lord's sannyasa, suffering in separation from Him, Madhava settled in Daihat and Vasudeva in Tamoluk; according to another, the brothers parted after Mahaprabhu's disappearance10.

Neither the day of Madhava's appearance, nor the day of his departure, nor the year and place where he left this world, nor the place of his samadhi is given by the sources; nor are his days in the Vaishnava calendar of the Sri Chaitanya Saraswat Math (it commemorates the departure of Govinda and of Vasudeva).

Yet the brothers' kirtana did not cease even after the Lord's disappearance. According to the “Bhakti-ratnakara” (wave 10), when Narottama Dasa sang at the great festival in Kheturi, Sri Chaitanya appeared there with His companions, and among them were Madhava Ghosha, Vasu Ghosha and Govinda Ghosha. Describing the companions' dance, the poet exclaims: "…the dance of Govinda, Madhava and Vasu Ghosha — who could have the composure to watch it?" (BR 10.549).

Significance

Madhava Ghosha is, in Vraja, the sakhi Rasollasa, who sang the songs of Sri Vishakha; Srila Bhaktisiddhanta sees in him a kaya-vyuha of Sri Radha. He descended into Gaura's pastimes to sing for the Lord. He belongs to both ganas: Mahaprabhu sent him with Nityananda, and in serving Nityananda in Gauda he served Gaura; and every year he returned to Nilachala to sing before the Lord and before Jagannatha's chariot. To his singing Sri Chaitanya and Nityananda danced, and his dana-khanda in the house of Gadadhara Dasa revealed an extraordinary bhava in Nityananda. Vrindavana Dasa called him "the singer of Vrindavana," and Srila Bhaktisiddhanta disclosed the meaning of these words: such is the kirtana of one in whom worldly conceptions have been destroyed completely and only one desire grows — to serve Hari.

Notes

  1. One biography refers here to verse 118 — a misprint for verse 188.
  2. One biography supports this information with a reference to the “Chaitanya-charitamrita,” Antya, ch. 5; in fact it then quotes the “Chaitanya-bhagavata” (Antya 5.257–259), where nothing is said about caste. The information on the kayasthas of northern Rarh comes from the “Anubhashya” on CC, Adi 10.115.
  3. Where exactly in Shrihatta — the accounts differ: according to one biography, the house of Vasudeva's maternal uncle stood in the village of Buran (Burangi); according to another, this is the brothers' native village (Baduna, or Burangi); according to one, the brothers moved to Navadvipa "later," according to another, after their father's death.
  4. According to one biography, Govinda is the eighty-second branch, Madhava the eighty-third and Vasudeva the eighty-fourth; in the subheadings of the edition of the “Chaitanya-charitamrita” with the “Anubhashya” the numbering is different: Govinda is the eighty-first branch, Madhava the eighty-second, Vasudeva the eighty-third. Another biography gives the reference to this verse with a misprint.
  5. According to the “Charitamrita,” the lead singer of the fourth group was Govinda, and Madhava and Vasudeva sang with him; so too the biographies, though one of them, in its chapter on Vasudeva, names Vasudeva "with his two brothers" as the lead singers. Another biography gives this account with a wrong reference to the Adi-lila instead of Madhya-lila 13.
  6. One biography presents these nine as the kirtana the Lord would form whenever He wished to dance, and, taking the first Govinda to be Govinda Ghosha, names him and the other eight. According to the “Charitamrita,” this was at the Ratha-yatra, and the nine were placed in the group of Svarupa Damodara; which Madhava this is, it does not specify.
  7. According to one account, Nityananda sat on the throne of Vishnu, according to another, on a couch; one biography says that Nityananda came to Raghava together with the three brothers. According to the “Chaitanya-charitamrita” (Adi 10.118), Govinda stayed with the Lord in Nilachala, while the “Chaitanya-bhagavata” names all three brothers in Panihati; the biographies do not discuss this. One of them calls CB, Antya 5.259 the passage on "the dance of the three brothers," but in the verse the brothers sing and Nityananda dances. Another, following the “Charitamrita,” says that to the brothers' singing both Sri Chaitanya and Nityananda danced in ecstasy.
  8. In the verse of the “Chaitanya-bhagavata” itself only Madhava is called "the singer of Vrindavana"; it is Srila Bhaktisiddhanta's commentary that extends the name to all three brothers.
  9. The biographies relate this lila differently. One says that Nityananda was among the spectators of a "performance" of the dana-lila given by Madhavananda Ghosha and fell into a deep trance; another, following the commentary of Srila Bhaktivedanta Swami, says that Madhava Ghosha "performed a drama," the “Dana-khanda,” with Nityananda and Gadadhara Dasa helping him. The basis of these words is Srila Bhaktisiddhanta's “Anubhashya” on CC, Adi 10.53: Madhava Ghosha, with the help of Nityananda and Dasa Gadadhara, sang and danced before the Deity of Gopala, enacting (abhinaya) the “Dana-khanda.” We follow the “Chaitanya-bhagavata”: Madhavananda sang, Nityananda danced. In every case this is no worldly show, but Krishna's lila revealed in kirtana and dance.
  10. One biography, in its chapter on the brothers, names Daihat as Madhava's shripata without reservation, while in its chapter on Vasudeva it gives this with the words "some say"; according to another, Madhava "eventually" settled in Dain-Hat; according to a third, the brothers parted after Mahaprabhu's departure, and Madhava Ghosha settled in Danihatta.
